video_title: AI, Higher Rates and the Next Big Economic Imbalance | Global Macro | Ep.107
gist: Matt Klein (author of The Overshoot, co-author of Trade Wars Are Class Wars) argues to host Alan Dunn that the AI capex boom is a reason for real interest rates to go UP, not down, because the 1990s productivity boom showed up as faster growth rather than disinflation — and that measured underlying US productivity has been roughly zero for 18+ months. He also argues US bond yields near current levels are justified by ~7% nominal growth rather than deficits, and that the real global imbalance story is China's trade surplus exploding from ~$100-200bn to over $1 trillion a year, with US tariff policy aimed at the wrong countries.

insights.claim: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech walked back fears that he would be a political 'hack', by explicitly restating the inflation target and conceding there is a gap between actual inflation and that target which policy must close.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Removes the 'captured Fed' tail risk that was being priced into the long end; front-end pricing should track inflation data rather than political-pressure narratives.

insights.claim: Market pricing after Jackson Hole shifted toward the Fed RAISING short-term rates rather than cutting, because inflation has made essentially no progress in roughly three years and Fed officials are only now accepting that the 2021-22 inflation impulse will not simply unwind on its own.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: A hiking-biased Fed against consensus cut expectations is the key asymmetry for front-end rates, steepeners, and duration-sensitive equities.
insights.quote: the market pricing reaction was pretty clear that the assumption okay maybe the Fed is going to raise short-term rates

insights.claim: Warsh's newly announced productivity-and-jobs task force is a red flag for reverse-engineered policy, because before his nomination he had already argued that AI would be inherently deflationary and would create scope for lower interest rates.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Watch whether the task force output is used to justify cuts on a productivity story the data does not yet support — that would be a credibility event for the long end.
insights.quote: there's a concern again trying to sort of predetermine the answer

insights.claim: Of all the Fed task forces, the balance-sheet task force (Raghuram Rajan, Jeremy Stein, Karen Dynan) is the one most likely to produce a genuine policy surprise, because it is the only question where current Fed officials' public views are genuinely unsettled and divided.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Balance-sheet framework changes move repo, bill supply and duration risk premia; this is the under-watched task force for rates traders.
insights.quote: the balance sheet tax force I think is very interesting uh potentially um just because of the caliber of people they have there and the nature of the question and the fact that it's really unsettled

insights.claim: There has still been no meaningful acceleration in measured US productivity despite the AI capex boom, so every bullish productivity-driven disinflation forecast is currently pure speculation rather than data.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Positions premised on an AI productivity miracle lowering inflation have no data support yet; the burden of proof sits with the bulls.
insights.quote: so far we've not actually seen any meaningful productivity acceleration in the data so far

insights.claim: The San Francisco Fed's decomposition of output per hour shows zero growth — possibly slightly negative — in underlying US productivity over the past 18-plus months, with all measured gains coming from workforce experience, more capital per worker and higher resource utilization.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
insights.so_what: If the gains are 'working harder' rather than 'working smarter', the economy has less non-inflationary headroom than headline productivity suggests — hawkish for rates.
insights.quote: so far it seems that people are working harder rather than smarter

insights.claim: Greenspan's reputation for calling the 1990s productivity boom early is overstated — he only began making the argument in mid-1996 and the productivity data did not accelerate until 1997, meaning today's AI productivity calls are far further ahead of the data than his were.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Removes the historical precedent policymakers lean on for pre-emptively easing into a productivity story.
insights.quote: He didn't start making that argument until the middle of 1996. So he he was in front of the official data but not radically in front of it

insights.claim: Even a full replay of the 1990s would imply higher, not lower, interest rates, because the level of rates entering the 1990s boom was substantially above today's, real rates rose once the boom started, and arguably they should have risen more than they did.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: The single most tradeable inversion in the episode: the consensus 'AI = disinflation = lower rates' trade may be backwards; favors short duration and long real yields.
insights.quote: even if you were to sort of naively say it's the same thing, the implication that interest rates would go down, I think is is not correct. I think it's very plausible that if that were to happen, interest rates would go up.

insights.claim: The 1990s productivity boom showed up almost entirely as faster real growth rather than lower inflation; what disinflation there was came from collapsing commodity prices during emerging-market crises, post-bubble Japan and a rising dollar — none of it productivity-driven.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Reframes the productivity trade as a nominal-growth trade, not a disinflation trade — bullish nominal GDP, bearish long bonds.
insights.quote: The productivity boom in the 90s mostly manifested as more growth rather than less inflation.

insights.claim: Today's disinflation forces run the opposite way to the 1990s: since Covid, the war in Ukraine and the war in Iran, countries are stockpiling physical goods and rebuilding domestic productive capacity, which is structurally more inflationary rather than less.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Supports a structurally higher inflation floor and argues against duration on any 'the 90s are back' analogy.

insights.claim: Higher productivity should raise, not lower, the cost of capital, because more attractive investment opportunities raise the demand for investment and expected returns relative to everything else.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: A clean mental model for why an AI boom is a bear case for bonds, not a bull case.

insights.claim: AI's productivity gains are so far concentrated in software engineering, which is only a small share of the economy, and historical technology diffusion (electric motors took decades) suggests economy-wide gains take far longer than the 12-36 month timelines investors are pricing.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Timing risk: even a genuine AI productivity boom may arrive years after the capex that is being underwritten on it.

insights.claim: Economy-wide productivity is not directly measurable — it is nominal spending deflated by an inflation measure and divided by estimated hours — so measurement error in any of the three inputs can manufacture apparent productivity swings, as it did when low-wage job losses in the pandemic mechanically inflated output per hour.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Guards against trading a policy pivot off a single productivity print; composition effects can fake a boom.

insights.claim: Treating AI as a separate factor of production changes nothing fundamental for economic models, because AI tokens can be handled as an intermediate input like energy, and because companies pay real money for AI services the national accounts already capture the value flow.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Deflates claims that AI makes existing macro data or models obsolete — a common justification for ignoring inflation data.
insights.quote: I might be very skeptical because I've seen this before of people saying this like new technologies changes our fundamental understanding of how the economy works

themes.theme: AI capex: real boom, foreign leakage

insights.claim: The AI data-center buildout is already showing up in consumer prices, most visibly through memory chips, with Apple raising MacBook and iPad prices by roughly 20% and consumer flash-drive and memory prices rising before that.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: A concrete inflation transmission channel from AI capex to core goods CPI — watch memory pricing as a leading indicator for consumer electronics inflation.
insights.quote: I think Apple just recently announced they're raising all the prices on their MacBooks and and iPads by like 20% or something

insights.claim: Most of the incremental US spend on data centers flows abroad as imports, with Taiwan and Korea the main beneficiaries, unlike the 1990s when the capex boom mostly translated into domestic US production.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: A US AI capex bust would hit equity valuations hard but domestic GDP less than headline capex numbers imply; the GDP exposure sits in Taiwan and Korea.
insights.quote: most of the incremental spend on data centers is actually flowing abroad

insights.claim: The view that the US economy is entirely dependent on AI is a misreading — the economy is growing for multiple reasons and AI is one impulse whose direct GDP contribution is diluted because so much of it leaks into higher net imports.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Argues against the 'ex-AI the US is in recession' framing that underpins many bearish macro positions.
insights.quote: the idea that the US economy is entirely dependent on AI growth I think is uh a misreading of what's been happening

insights.claim: The 1990s were a genuine broad-based real investment boom, not merely a valuation bubble — real net investment saw its biggest sustained boom since the data began around 1929, and industrial capacity growth was unprecedented back to the 1940s even excluding high-tech sectors like semis and computers.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Undercuts the comfort that 'this time it's real capex, not a dot-com valuation bubble' — the 1990s were real capex too, and still busted.

insights.claim: The 2000s downturn was worse than commonly appreciated because the collapse in business investment was so large that the Fed offset it with an unsustainable housing bubble and still only produced anemic growth — a genuine risk template for an AI capex unwind.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: The second-order risk of an AI capex bust is not just the drawdown but the distortionary policy response that follows it.

insights.claim: Locking in a 5% fixed nominal return for 30 years makes no sense while the economy is growing around 7% a year in dollar terms — it only makes sense if you believe nominal growth is about to fall toward 3%.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: A simple valuation test for long duration: buying the long bond is an explicit bet on a nominal growth collapse, not a neutral position.
insights.quote: if you think the growth is going to stay around 7% for a while, which it might not, but if you do, 5% makes no sense

insights.claim: The 10-year Treasury yield has been rangebound with no trend since mid-2023 and has not broken 5%, even though the 30-year has pushed higher — so the 'yields are surging' narrative is really a long-end/term-premium story.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein and host Alan Dunn
insights.so_what: Frames the trade as curve steepening and term premium rather than an outright level move in the belly.
insights.quote: the 10-year yields basically been in a rangebound for the past 3 years right if you look at a chart since like mid 2023 to now it's no trend whatsoever

insights.claim: Rising yields are a benign sign rather than a crisis signal — they reflect an economy that has escaped the post-financial-crisis regime, and the fact that they are the highest in 19 years mostly reflects how terrible many of those intervening years were.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Argues against the reflexive 'high yields will break something' trade; supports risk assets alongside higher rates.
insights.quote: there are worlds where interest rates go up um and it's not bad. I think this is one of those times.

insights.claim: Japan's 10-year yield hitting a 30-year high is the correct market response to Japan finally escaping deflation, not a signal of distress — rates should be different when people stop believing Japan will shrink toward zero forever.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Reframes the JGB selloff as a regime normalization rather than a funding crisis — relevant for carry-trade and global term-premium spillover trades.

insights.claim: The bond term-premium channel from deficits runs only through nominal growth, not through default risk, because the central bank in the US, UK, Japan or New Zealand can always finance the government — the risk deficits create is inflation, not default.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Directs attention away from 'bond vigilante default' narratives toward inflation breakevens as the correct expression of fiscal risk.

insights.claim: There is no policy combination for a large economy that lowers the budget deficit AND lowers interest rates without hitting growth — tax hikes and spending cuts lower rates only by lowering nominal growth; the exchange-rate-depreciation escape hatch used by Canada, Sweden and Norway in the early 1990s is unavailable to the US.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Kills the 'fiscal consolidation is a free lunch for bonds' trade — a credible consolidation is a growth-negative, risk-asset-negative event.
insights.quote: I don't think there's sort of this this magical independent thing you can do that would lower the budget deficit lower interest rates not hit growth

insights.claim: The rise in US government borrowing is the mirror image of unusually conservative private-sector behaviour: households and businesses are spending more than in the 2010s but not borrowing to finance it, so private indebtedness is falling while public borrowing rises.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Deficit-driven doom scenarios miss that aggregate leverage has shifted sectors, not exploded — argues against a private credit blowup thesis on leverage grounds.

insights.claim: US nominal growth (G) still exceeds the interest rate (R), but the primary deficit excluding interest is large enough that debt still grows relative to the economy regardless.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Precise framing for debt watchers: the binding variable is the primary deficit, not the R-vs-G spread everyone quotes.
insights.quote: the deficit excluding interest is big enough that it doesn't matter

insights.claim: US debt service costs relative to the economy are still below their early-1990s peak, because much outstanding debt was locked in at low rates and 1980s rates were far higher — though debt service will rise as low-coupon debt rolls.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Provides the timing edge: the interest-cost problem is a rolling-maturity story with years to run, not an imminent cliff.

insights.claim: So long as the rest of the world in aggregate runs a current account surplus, somebody in the US must be a net seller of financial assets — and it is better for that seller to be the government, which has the lowest cost of capital and least rollover risk, than the private sector.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: A genuinely non-consensus defense of large US deficits: cutting them without fixing the external imbalance just relocates leverage into riskier private balance sheets.
insights.quote: surely it is better for the entity selling financial assets to be the government, which is going to have the lowest cost of capital, the least risk of being able to roll anything over

insights.claim: The bad debt equilibrium to watch for is the Brazil scenario — extraordinarily high real interest rates and balanced primary budgets but crushing interest costs, a legacy of past hyperinflation episodes — and the US is nowhere near it.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete benchmark for what genuine fiscal distress looks like, so investors can avoid mispricing US fiscal risk against it.

insights.claim: China's aggregate trade surplus has expanded from roughly $100-200 billion a year pre-pandemic to over $1 trillion a year, an unprecedented shift for an economy of its size relative to the global economy ex-China.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: The single biggest macro imbalance number in the episode — it is the source of deflationary pressure on European manufacturing and the trigger for the next tariff wave.
insights.quote: China's trade surplus in the aggregate has increased from something on the order of a hundred billion to200 billion a year on the eve of the pandemic to over a trillion dollars a year

insights.claim: Chinese household consumption as a share of what China produces is lower than in any comparable society ever — the only analogues are corporate tax havens with inflated GDP, oil sheikhdoms, and the Soviet Union under Stalin.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Quantifies why Chinese rebalancing is structural, not cyclical — a reason to discount every 'China stimulus will fix demand' rally.

insights.claim: China's pandemic response was the inverse of the rest of the world's: rather than supporting consumers, it forced an estimated 50-70 million rural migrants out of cities and back to subsistence farming with no unemployment eligibility, and channelled stimulus into manufacturing capacity and export subsidies instead.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Explains the mechanism behind the export surge — excess capacity built deliberately, so it will not self-correct with a cyclical recovery.
insights.quote: the number of people who were migrants from the countryside to cities fell something on the order of 50 to 70 million people during the initial lockdowns in 2020

insights.claim: Global imbalances matter for two specific reasons: they reveal distributional problems where people live below their means, and they correspond to increases in indebtedness that threaten financial stability — the same pattern seen before the global financial crisis and in the 1920s.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: A checklist for deciding when a current-account imbalance is benign versus a pre-crisis signal.

insights.claim: Borrowing to finance current spending is categorically different from borrowing to buy productive assets, because the former must be continually rolled and creates no future value — the distinction that makes an imbalance dangerous.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: A credit-quality lens for judging whether a rising debt stock is a red flag or a rational investment cycle.

insights.claim: The cleanest resolution of the imbalance is for Chinese households to spend more on themselves, which is already the Chinese government's official position and a live debate among Chinese academics — it simply has not been prioritised enough to move the numbers.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Watch for a genuine Chinese consumption policy shift as the highest-impact, lowest-probability positive catalyst for global growth and EU industrials.
insights.quote: The cleanest answer is for people in China to spend more on themselves to increase their own living standards. Everyone will be better off if they do that.

themes.theme: Tariffs aimed at the wrong targets

insights.claim: US trade policy over the past 18 months does not correspond to the actual data on global imbalances — most tariff energy has been spent on countries that contribute nothing to global imbalances, while China has comparatively been let off the hook.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Implies the tariff regime is less economically binding on China than headlines suggest — and that the real China trade shock still lies ahead, likely from Europe.
insights.quote: it seems like most of the energy the US has expended in terms of tariffs and trade conflict have been with countries that are not contributing global imbalances

insights.claim: US-China business conditions are reported by people on the ground in China as better than they have been in a very long time and much better than in 2023-2024, which is the opposite of what the political rhetoric would suggest.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: A contrarian ground-truth data point for China-exposed multinationals versus the headline geopolitical risk premium.
insights.quote: he said that he thought that the business climate and US China relations now or like as of you know a month ago whatever two months ago was better than it had been in a very long time

insights.claim: Europe is the more likely source of the next major China trade action, because Chinese exports of motor vehicles and chemicals are hitting European industry acutely, and a reasonable estimate that the yuan is ~35% undervalued gives Europe a template for sectoral tariffs of 35-40%.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: A specific, sizeable and under-priced tariff scenario: European autos and chemicals are the sectors to watch for policy protection.
insights.quote: if you take sort of I think a very reasonable estimate that that the Chinese yuan is undervalued on the order of 35%

insights.claim: Tariffs are a leaky instrument versus the exchange rate, because the first Trump administration's China tariffs mostly caused rerouting — direct US imports from China fell sharply while imports from Southeast Asian countries rose, leaving the net effect minimal.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Expect the same rerouting if Europe tariffs China — favours Southeast Asian transshipment beneficiaries over the tariff-protected domestic incumbents.

insights.claim: A Plaza Accord 2.0 with China is a non-starter regardless of its economic merits, because the Chinese believe the 1985 Plaza Accord was a trick the US played to destroy Japan as a rival great power — and they believe it worked.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Fade any currency-accord rally in the yuan or Asian FX; the political constraint, not the economics, is binding.
insights.quote: the Chinese believe that this was essentially a trick that the US played on Japan to destroy them and and take them out of the running as being another great power and they think that it worked

insights.claim: The US Treasury's yen intervention was economically trivial — despite a widely photographed note suggesting $5-10 billion of yen purchases, reported data suggests only about $500 million was actually bought, a rounding error versus FX market size.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Treat the intervention as signalling rather than flow — it should not be extrapolated into a sustained USD/JPY policy floor.
insights.quote: my former colleagues at FD Alphaville wrote that as of the data that we can see, assuming they reported everything correctly, they bought only 500 million

insights.claim: The likely motive for the US yen intervention was to stop Japan from selling its dollar assets, because the Treasury Secretary fears anything that pushes US Treasury yields higher — which is also why the Fed's securities-lending facility was promoted as an alternative to outright Japanese Treasury sales.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Reveals a policy put on Treasury yields operating through FX channels — a key constraint to watch if Japanese official selling resumes.
insights.quote: I think it's just that he has this fear of anything making Treasury yields go up

insights.claim: Japan has enormous unused ammunition to strengthen the yen: roughly $1 trillion of official FX reserves plus far larger foreign currency assets across public sector entities, all bought when the yen was much more expensive, so selling them for yen would book an immediate massive profit.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: A large latent yen-appreciation catalyst that is politically, not financially, constrained — asymmetric risk for anyone short yen.

insights.claim: The yen has failed to appreciate despite a large rise in Japanese long-end yields because that yield move coincided with a shift higher in Japanese inflation and growth expectations, so the forward-looking real rate change was smaller than the nominal move implied.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Explains why the standard rate-differential FX model has failed on USD/JPY and warns against re-running it on the next BoJ hike.

insights.claim: Japanese non-financial corporate profits have been massively inflated relative to operating profits over the past six years by interest income on huge portfolios of foreign interest-bearing assets, so a sharp rise in Japanese rates or a stronger yen would hit reported earnings through that channel.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: A non-obvious earnings-quality risk in Japanese equities: profits are partly a carry trade, vulnerable to BoJ normalization and yen strength.

insights.claim: The Korean won is an even more obvious candidate than the yen for being too cheap against the dollar, yet no intervention has occurred there.
insights.speaker: Matt Klein, author of The Overshoot
insights.so_what: Flags KRW as the under-watched appreciation candidate if dollar-weakening policy broadens beyond Japan.
